clinicalPearls: A pyogranulomatous disease acquired by inhaling Blastomyces conidia or hyphal fragments from disturbed soil; typically a pulmonary infection, with a subset progressing to disseminated disease involving skin, bone, brain, or genitourinary system (p.1699).
A primary fungal pathogen: it infects persons with intact as well as impaired immune systems (p.1699).

Endemic mainly in North America (Mississippi/Ohio and St. Lawrence River basins, Great Lakes states, southeastern states) but of global importance with cases in Africa and Asia; outbreaks linked to construction, soil excavation, water sports, compost piles, and beaver dams (p.1699-1700).
Yeast form (37 degrees C) is a broad-based budding yeast, 4-29 micrometers, with a doubly refractile cell wall, allowing distinction from other fungi (p.1700, 1702).
After a 3-week to 3-month incubation, about 50% of those exposed develop symptomatic infection; the long incubation means cases present year-round (p.1701).

Pulmonary disease occurs in 69-93% of symptomatic patients (most common feature) and may present as asymptomatic infection, influenza-like illness, acute pneumonia, chronic pneumonia, or ARDS (p.1701).
Disseminated disease occurs in 15-48%; skin is the most common site (papules, ulcers, verrucous lesions, abscesses), followed by bone (osteomyelitis of spine, long bones, ribs) (p.1701).
CNS (meningitis/abscess/mass), laryngeal, and genitourinary (prostate, epididymis) dissemination each occur in fewer than 10%, usually with concurrent lung or skin involvement (p.1701).

Diagnosis combines microscopy of stained specimens, fungal culture, and antigen testing; serology (complement fixation 9%, immunodiffusion 28%) is diagnostically dispensable, though a newer anti-BAD1 antibody test has higher sensitivity/specificity (p.1702).
Urine galactomannan antigen testing (sensitivity 85-93% urine, 57-82% serum) has supplanted older serology and can monitor treatment response as levels decline (p.1702-1703).
Treatment is recommended for ALL patients because there are no criteria to identify which untreated cases will self-resolve; antifungals are amphotericin B formulations and triazoles (p.1699, 1703).
harrison.pathophysiology: Blastomyces is a thermally dimorphic species complex (including B. dermatitidis, B. gilchristii, B. helicus, B. percursus, B. emzantsi). In soil at 22-25 degrees C it grows as septate hyphae producing infectious conidia; inhalation into the lungs and conversion at the mammalian core temperature of 37 degrees C yields a pathogenic broad-based budding yeast that upregulates yeast-phase virulence factors and downregulates host immune defenses, eliciting pyogranulomatous inflammation. Shared virulence traits with other dimorphic fungi (Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Sporothrix, Paracoccidioides) include thermotolerance at 37 degrees C, intracellular survival, and the ability to infect immunocompetent hosts. Blastomyces can also replicate outside macrophages. Notably, immunosuppression has only minimal influence on dissemination, suggesting fungal virulence factors outweigh host defenses; the infecting species and duration of pulmonary symptoms (and concomitant AIDS) influence dissemination, with B. dermatitidis more likely to disseminate than B. gilchristii. (p.1700-1702)
infectionMimics: Histoplasmosis (B. helicus small yeast can be confused with Histoplasma; antigen cross-reactivity with H. capsulatum, Paracoccidioides, T. marneffei) (p.1702-1703)
additionalInvestigations: Microscopy of stained clinical specimens for broad-based budding yeast with doubly refractile cell wall (sputum, tracheal aspirate, BAL fluid, or purulent drainage stained with calcofluor, 10% KOH, or Papanicolaou; sensitivity 50-90%) (p.1702)

Histopathology of tissue stained with Gomori methenamine silver or periodic acid-Schiff, assessed for pyogranulomatous inflammation and broad-based budding yeast (Gram and H&E do not visualize the yeast well) (p.1702)
Fungal culture on special media (Sabouraud dextrose, potato dextrose, brain-heart infusion); 5-28 days incubation; definitive diagnosis (p.1702)
Chemiluminescent DNA probe or PCR to confirm identification (does not distinguish among species) (p.1702)
Urine, serum, BAL, and CSF galactomannan antigen testing (urine sensitivity 85-93%, serum 57-82%); useful to monitor response (p.1702-1703)
redFlags: Unexplained respiratory failure or ARDS in a person from or visiting an endemic area; 4-15% of pulmonary cases develop ARDS with a fulminant course and 40-89% mortality (p.1701)
Pneumonia that fails to improve despite antibiotics, or pneumonia with extrapulmonary features (skin lesions, osteomyelitis, CNS involvement) (p.1701)
Skin ulcers unresponsive to standard therapy (p.1701)
AIDS with CD4+ count <100/microliter: increased risk of CNS dissemination (p.1702)
B. helicus infection (commonly causes fungemia, usually in immunosuppressed hosts, high mortality ~71%) (p.1702)
harrison.prognosis: Overall mortality ranges from 5 to 13% (7.9% in 11,776 U.S. hospital admissions, 2010-2020), with most deaths from respiratory failure due to ARDS. Mortality is higher in older patients and those with COPD or concomitant solid/hematologic malignancy, and is increased when diagnosis is delayed. The vast majority who recover from pulmonary blastomycosis do not have long-term loss of pulmonary function; cutaneous blastomycosis typically heals with scarring. (p.1703)
pitfalls: Called 'the great pretender' because it mimics infectious and noninfectious diseases; pulmonary blastomycosis is commonly misdiagnosed, and patients often receive two or three antibiotic courses before diagnosis (p.1701).

No distinctive radiographic features differentiate blastomycosis from other pulmonary diseases (consolidation, mass, nodules, miliary, cavitary patterns all possible); a mass lesion can mimic malignancy (p.1701).

Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion and a detailed exposure history (about 50-60% of patients have environmental risk factors); failure to consider Blastomyces in the differential delays treatment (p.1701).
Serology by complement fixation/immunodiffusion has poor sensitivity and is diagnostically dispensable (p.1702).
Echinocandins are ineffective (minimal beta-(1,3)-glucan in the yeast cell wall) and should not be used (p.1703).
Antigen testing cross-reacts with other dimorphic fungi, notably H. capsulatum which shares the same endemic region (p.1703).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not give a formal numeric severity scale. Severe blastomycosis is operationally defined as disease requiring hospitalization (medical ward, intermediate care, or ICU). Risk factors for severe pulmonary disease include diabetes, solid organ transplantation, immunosuppression, and multilobar pneumonia; ARDS (in 4-15%) represents the most severe pulmonary form with high mortality. Special high-risk/severity categories warranting intensified management include CNS, severe pulmonary, and severe disseminated disease. (p.1701-1703)
management: Antifungal therapy is the mainstay — an oral azole such as itraconazole for mild-to-moderate disease
Liposomal amphotericin B for severe, disseminated, central-nervous-system or life-threatening pulmonary disease, followed by step-down azole consolidation
Prolonged treatment courses with therapeutic drug-level monitoring of azoles to ensure adequate exposure
Respiratory support, including for acute respiratory distress syndrome, in severe pulmonary blastomycosis
Monitor treatment response with serial urine and serum antigen testing alongside clinical assessment
Intensify and extend therapy in immunocompromised patients and adapt agent choice in pregnancy, with specialist infectious-diseases input
